intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. The notes under each slide explain it, tell you what to remember and warn you where people slip. Work the exercises in pencil, check yourself against the questions, and write your own notes in the space around mine.

sections.title: What the BRSR is and why it exists
sections.big_idea: A company's accounts say what it earned. The BRSR says what it did to water, workers and air, **in one format** you can compare.
in_plain_words: Before 2012 an Indian company could publish glowing pages about itself, and no two reports could be set side by side. SEBI moved in steps: voluntary guidelines, a report for the top 100 companies, then a stricter format for 1,000.

Two kinds of people use the result. **Preparers** need to know what each question asks and how to calculate it. **Readers**, such as investors, NGOs and journalists, need to know where to look and when a figure deserves a question.

events.what: Assessment or assurance; value chain voluntary

diagram.caption: the staircase from guideline to checked numbers

key_terms.meaning: Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report, part of the annual report.
SEBI's listing regulations, the legal home of the BRSR.
The nine principles of responsible business conduct, used as the BRSR's skeleton.
A spending duty under the Companies Act, separate from the BRSR.

worked_example.title: Put the events in order
worked_example.setup: A colleague gives you five labels on slips of paper. Which comes first?
steps: The labels are: BRSR Core, BRR for the top 100, NVGs, BRSR for the top 1,000, assessment or assurance.
Start with the only voluntary item: the NVGs of 2011.
Next comes the first compulsory report, the BRR of 2012.
Then the BRSR of 2021, mandatory from FY 2022-23.
Then Core in 2023 and assessment or assurance in 2025.
worked_example.answer: NVGs, BRR, BRSR, BRSR Core, assessment or assurance.

mistakes: Treating CSR, BRSR and ESG as three words for the same thing. They are three different obligations or labels.
Reading a BRSR as proof. It is the company's own statement in a regulated format.
Using the format of one year to read another. It changed in 2021, 2023 and 2025.

recall.q: Which regulation requires the BRSR?
recall.a: SEBI (LODR) Regulations 2015, Regulation 34(2)(f).

recall.q: From which financial year was the BRSR mandatory for the top 1,000?
Give one thing a BRSR can tell you and one thing it cannot.
recall.a: It can show the company's own figures for two years side by side. It cannot show whether figures outside BRSR Core were checked by anyone.

recall.q: What is the difference between CSR and BRSR?
recall.a: CSR is a spending duty under s135 of the Companies Act. The BRSR is a disclosure under SEBI's rules.

sections.title: Who must file, and from when
sections.big_idea: Rank by market value decides who files. **Top 1,000 must, everyone else may.**
in_plain_words: Regulation 34(2)(f) names the top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalisation. The stock exchanges draw the list using an average over July to December, which stops a few lucky trading days from changing who is in.

Inside the report, **essential indicators are compulsory** and leadership indicators are voluntary. When you compare companies, start with the essential ones, because a leadership row one company answers and another skips cannot be compared.

diagram.root: Must this company file a BRSR?
diagram.caption: coverage in one look

key_terms.meaning: Share price times shares; the ranking uses a July to December average.
A question every covered company must answer.
A question a company may leave blank.
An added condition attached to a rule.

worked_example.title: A company ranked 640th
worked_example.setup: It is listed and ranked 640 by average market capitalisation.
steps: Is it listed? Yes. Is it in the top 1,000? Yes. So it must file.
Find where rank 640 falls in the Core timetable.
Top 150 from FY 2023-24, top 250 from FY 2024-25, top 500 from FY 2025-26, top 1,000 from FY 2026-27.
Rank 640 is outside the top 500 but inside the top 1,000.
worked_example.answer: It must file, and its Core figures must be checked from FY 2026-27.

mistakes: Assuming an unlisted company must file because it owes CSR. The two duties are separate.
Forgetting that the top 1,000 list is redrawn, so rank can change year to year.
Comparing a leadership indicator one company answered with a blank from another.

recall.q: How is the top 1,000 ranked today?
recall.a: By average market capitalisation from 1 July to 31 December of each year.

recall.q: What did the 28 March 2025 circular change in the wording?
recall.a: "Assurance" became "assessment or assurance".

recall.q: Who may file a BRSR voluntarily?
recall.a: Listed entities outside the top 1,000, including SME-listed ones; high value debt listed entities under Reg 62Q(3).

recall.q: Which kind of indicator should you compare first across companies?
recall.a: Essential indicators.

sections.title: Sections A, B and C and the nine principles
sections.big_idea: Every BRSR has three parts: **who the company is, what it promises, and what the numbers say.**
in_plain_words: Section A is general disclosure, and its point 13 says whether the report covers the company alone or the group. That one choice changes every figure after it, so read it first.

Section B lists policies against nine principles and asks who oversees them. Section C is where the numbers live, principle by principle, with essential indicators first. **Always read both the current and previous year columns.**

diagram.caption: who, what it promises, what the numbers say

key_terms.meaning: The report covers the company alone.
The report covers the company and its group.
One of nine statements from the NGRBC that Sections B and C follow.
The company's own list of material issues, in Section A.

worked_example.title: Where does each figure live?
worked_example.setup: Place each figure under its principle.
steps: Groundwater withdrawn by a plant: environment, so P6.
Complaints under the POSH Act: human rights, so P5.
Share of inputs bought from MSMEs: inclusive growth, so P8.
Days of accounts payable: fair dealing with suppliers, so P1.

mistakes: Reading Section C before checking the boundary in Section A, point 13.
Taking a policy in Section B as proof of behaviour. Section C shows results.
Reading only the current year's column.

recall.q: What does Section B ask about?
recall.a: The company's policies against each of the nine principles and who approved and oversees them.

recall.q: Under which principle do energy, water and waste figures sit?
recall.a: Principle 6.

recall.q: Which principle covers human rights and POSH complaints?
recall.a: Principle 5.

recall.q: Why read Section A, point 13 first?
recall.a: It says whether figures cover the company alone or the group.

sections.title: BRSR Core and assessment or assurance
sections.big_idea: BRSR Core is the **short list of figures that must be independently checked.** Trust these most.
in_plain_words: SEBI picked nine attributes, defined how each is measured and set a timetable that starts with the largest 150 companies and reaches the top 1,000 in FY 2026-27. Scope 3 is not in Core.
The checker may be an assessor or an assurer, working to Industry Standards Forum standards. The checker must be independent: the firm that **advised on the report cannot also check it**.

diagram.caption: the Core checking timetable: one year, one wider circle

key_terms.meaning: A subset of BRSR figures with defined KPIs and a checking timetable.
Third-party checking to ISF standards, added in 2025.
The older word, linked to accountancy standards.
Industry Standards Forum: ASSOCHAM, CII and FICCI.

worked_example.title: Which year, which company?
worked_example.setup: Four listed companies are ranked 120th, 240th, 470th and 910th.
steps: Rank 120 is inside the top 150, so FY 2023-24.
Rank 240 is inside the top 250 but outside 150, so FY 2024-25.
Rank 470 is inside the top 500, so FY 2025-26.
Rank 910 needs the top 1,000, so FY 2026-27.

mistakes: Believing Scope 3 is in BRSR Core. It is a leadership indicator.
Hiring the consultant who prepared the report to check its Core figures.
Assuming figures outside Core were checked.

recall.q: How many attributes does BRSR Core have?
recall.a: Nine.

recall.q: Name two of the attributes that are not about the environment.
recall.a: Any two of: employee wellbeing and safety, gender diversity, inclusive development, fairness with customers and suppliers, open-ness of business.

recall.q: Where in Section A do you see who assessed or assured?
recall.a: Point 14 names the provider and point 15 gives the type.

recall.q: What conflict rule applies to the provider?
recall.a: It must not sell non-assessment services, including consulting, to the listed entity or its group.

sections.title: Greenhouse gas accounting
sections.big_idea: Emissions are **three multiplications** whose errors hide in the inputs.
in_plain_words: Take activity data, such as litres of diesel or MWh of power. Multiply by an emission factor, then by a warming potential for gases other than CO2. The result is tonnes of CO2 equivalent.

Scope 1 is what the company burns, Scope 2 is the power it buys, Scope 3 is the rest of the chain. India's own grid factor from the CEA changes every year, so **a stale factor gives a wrong answer that looks right**.

diagram.note: check units, factor year and boundary before you trust the answer

key_terms.meaning: Direct emissions from sources the company owns or controls.
Emissions from purchased electricity, heat, cooling and steam.
Global warming potential, used to express other gases as CO2e.
Emissions divided by a measure of output, such as revenue.

worked_example.title: Scope 2 with the right and wrong factor
worked_example.setup: A plant buys 5,000 MWh of grid electricity in FY 2024-25. Use 0.710 t CO2 per MWh.
steps: Suppose the team used the FY 2023-24 factor 0.727 by mistake.
The error is 3,635 minus 3,550 = 85 t, which is about 2.4% of 3,550.
worked_example.answer: 3,550 t; the wrong factor overstates it by 85 t, about 2.4%.

mistakes: Entering kWh where the sheet asks for MWh, which inflates Scope 2 a thousand times.
Using a CEA factor from an old version or the wrong year.
Calling a partial Scope 3 total the whole Scope 3 without listing the categories counted.

recall.q: Which scope covers bought grid electricity?
recall.a: Scope 2.

recall.q: What does the CEA grid factor give you?
recall.a: Tonnes of CO2 per MWh for India's grid, which you multiply by MWh bought.

recall.q: Why does the GWP edition matter?
recall.a: Methane's value differs between IPCC editions, so state which you used.

recall.q: Can intensity fall while total emissions rise?
recall.a: Yes, if revenue grows faster than emissions.

sections.title: Energy, water and waste
sections.big_idea: Convert to **one unit** (GJ, kL, tonnes), add carefully, then divide by revenue.
in_plain_words: Energy is a six-cell table: renewable and non-renewable electricity, fuel and other. Convert everything to GJ (1 MWh is 3.6 GJ) before you add, and count a captive plant's fuel once only.

Water has withdrawal, consumption and discharge. Waste has eight categories, each split into recovered and disposed. For all three, **recovered plus disposed should equal generated**, so a gap means stock on site or an error.

key_terms.meaning: Gigajoule. 1 MWh equals 3.6 GJ.
Withdrawal minus discharge, when not metered directly.
Recycled, re-used or other recovery.
Incinerated, landfilled or other disposal.

worked_example.title: Energy and renewable share
worked_example.setup: A plant buys 1,000 MWh of grid power, makes 100 MWh from its own rooftop solar and burns diesel worth 500 GJ.
steps: Grid: 1,000 × 3.6 = 3,600 GJ (non-renewable electricity).
Solar: 100 × 3.6 = 360 GJ (renewable electricity).
Diesel: 500 GJ (non-renewable fuel).
Renewable share = 360 ÷ 4,460 = 8.1%.

mistakes: Adding MWh and GJ without converting.
Counting the fuel and the electricity it generates, so the same energy appears twice.
Quoting a national water total when the plant sits in a water-stressed area.

recall.q: How many GJ are in one MWh?
How do you estimate water consumption if it is not metered?
recall.a: Withdrawal minus discharge.

recall.q: How many waste categories does the format use?
recall.a: Eight, from plastic waste to other non-hazardous waste.

recall.q: Which scheme sets energy targets for large plants?
recall.a: The Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme.

sections.title: Employees, communities and customers
sections.big_idea: People figures are **ratios**, and the denominator decides what they mean.
in_plain_words: Wellbeing spending is divided by revenue. Safety is expressed as the lost-time injury frequency rate. Wages for women are a share of total wages. Sourcing from small producers is a share of input value.

The BRSR asks for employees and workers separately, because **contract workers often carry more risk**. A blended rate can hide a higher rate for the people most at risk, so always look for the split before you accept a safety figure.

diagram.note: a rate on a 200,000 hour base is one-fifth of this one

key_terms.meaning: Lost-time injury frequency rate, per million hours worked.
The law on sexual harassment of women at the workplace.
Micro, small and medium enterprise.
Payables times 365, divided by procurement cost.

worked_example.title: Injury rate on two bases
steps: Check: 0.24 is one-fifth of 1.2.
worked_example.answer: 1.2 on the BRSR base; the same injuries read 0.24 on a 200,000 hour base.

mistakes: Comparing an LTIFR on a 200,000 hour base with one on a million.
Reading a safety record for permanent staff as the record for everyone on site.
Treating zero POSH complaints as proof of a safe workplace.

recall.q: What is the base for the BRSR's LTIFR?
recall.a: One million hours worked.

recall.q: Why does the BRSR ask for employees and workers separately?
recall.a: Workers, often on contract, may face higher risk that a blended figure hides.

recall.q: What are the BRSR Core people figures for gender?
recall.a: Gross wages paid to women as a share of total wages, and POSH complaints.

recall.q: What does a rising figure of days payable tell small suppliers?
recall.a: They wait longer to be paid.

sections.title: Value chain and green credits
sections.big_idea: The value chain reaches suppliers and buyers, but since 2025 it is **voluntary**.
in_plain_words: A value chain partner is a supplier or buyer making up 2% or more of purchases or sales by value. The 2025 circular made disclosure and checking voluntary, so many companies will not report.

Green credits are a voluntary leadership indicator under Principle 6. Look for both the credits and the company's own emission cuts, because **one cannot stand in for the other**. A company can hold credits and still burn more fuel each year.

diagram.caption: how a partner is picked and how far disclosure goes

key_terms.meaning: A supplier or buyer at or above 2% of purchases or sales.
The share of purchases and sales the disclosure covers.
Money spent multiplied by an average factor.
A credit under India's Green Credit Programme.

worked_example.title: Who is a value chain partner?
worked_example.setup: Suppliers by share of purchases: 28%, 20%, 10%, 5% and 1.8%, with many small ones below that.
steps: A partner is at or above 2% individually.
The first four pass: 28, 20, 10 and 5.
The 1.8% supplier is below 2% and does not count.

mistakes: Calling green credits mandatory. They are a voluntary leadership indicator.
Reading figures for 40% of purchases as if they described the whole chain.
Quoting a spend-based Scope 3 estimate as measured data.

recall.q: What share makes a supplier a value chain partner?
recall.a: 2% or more of purchases or sales by value, individually.

recall.q: Is value chain disclosure compulsory today?
recall.a: No, it became voluntary under the 28 March 2025 circular.

recall.q: What is a green credit disclosure?
recall.a: Principle 6 leadership indicator 8: credits generated or procured by the entity and its top ten partners.

recall.q: Why check the coverage share?
recall.a: Figures for a small share of the chain say little about the rest.

sections.title: Materiality and the global frameworks
sections.big_idea: Ask **two questions** of every issue: does it affect the company, and does the company affect others?
in_plain_words: Financial materiality looks outside-in: what could change the company's cash flows. Double materiality adds the company's impact on people and the environment. BRSR question 26 asks for risks and opportunities to the business and does not name the test.

GRI is built on impacts. The ISSB standards are for investors, and as of October 2026 the deck found no Indian adoption. CBAM is an EU duty on imports of covered goods that reaches Indian exporters through their buyers.

left.title: Financial materiality
items: Asks: does it move cash flows?
Used by IFRS S1 and investors

right.title: Double materiality
items: Adds impact on people and nature
Asks: what do we do to others?

key_terms.meaning: Whether an issue is important enough to report.
Global Reporting Initiative, built around impacts.
International Sustainability Standards Board, issuer of IFRS S1 and S2.
The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism.

worked_example.title: Embedded emissions for CBAM
worked_example.setup: A mill exports 1,000 t of steel products. Verified emissions are 2.1 t CO2 per tonne of product.
steps: Embedded emissions = 1,000 × 2.1 = 2,100 t CO2.
The EU importer declares 2,100 t.
The certificates it surrenders are then reduced by a carbon price paid in the country of origin and by free allocation to EU producers.
The 2.1 figure is invented; real values come from monitoring.
worked_example.answer: 2,100 t declared; certificates are lower by the two adjustments.

mistakes: Saying the BRSR requires double materiality. The format does not say so.
Telling a client that India has adopted the ISSB standards without checking.
Treating CBAM plant data as the same as BRSR company totals.

recall.q: Which dimension does double materiality add to financial materiality?
recall.a: Impact on people and the environment.

recall.q: Which issue in a cement company is financial only: a carbon price on exports or dust harming a village?
recall.a: The carbon price. Dust is an impact issue, and financial too if it leads to closure orders.

recall.q: Who pays CBAM?
recall.a: The EU importer, who then asks the exporter for embedded emissions.

recall.q: Why does PPP adjustment matter between two Indian companies?
recall.a: It does not. It changes both figures by the same factor.

sections.title: Reading a BRSR critically
sections.big_idea: Five questions, **asked before you read the story**, catch most problems.
in_plain_words: The order matters. Boundary first, because standalone and group are different populations. Checking second, because it tells you how far to trust the rest. Movement from last year third, because errors often show up as a jump between the two columns.

Then check units and methods, and list the leadership indicators left blank. Remember that **intensity can fall while the total rises**, so ask for both figures. A claim that quotes only one of them deserves a second look.

key_terms.meaning: The set of entities the report covers.
A goal per unit of revenue or output. It puts no cap on total emissions.
A credit bought to balance emissions elsewhere.
A pattern that calls for a question. It proves nothing by itself.

worked_example.title: Intensity down, total up
worked_example.setup: Scope 1 and 2 rise from 1,000 t to 1,080 t. Revenue rises from Rs 400 crore to Rs 480 crore.
steps: Old intensity = 1,000 ÷ 400 = 2.5 t per crore.
New intensity = 1,080 ÷ 480 = 2.25 t per crore.
Change in intensity = 2.25 ÷ 2.5 minus 1 = minus 10%.
Change in total = 1,080 ÷ 1,000 minus 1 = plus 8%.
worked_example.answer: Intensity fell 10% while total emissions rose 8%. Report both.

mistakes: Comparing companies from different sectors on emission intensity.
Accepting a "carbon neutral" claim that rests on offsets alone.
Writing a proposal to a company without quoting its own figures.

recall.q: What are the five questions, in order?
recall.a: Boundary, checking, movement from last year, units and methods, blanks.

recall.q: Why can an intensity target be met while emissions rise?
recall.a: Because revenue can grow faster than emissions.

recall.q: Which part of Section A should an NGO read before approaching a company?
recall.a: Part VI (CSR details) and question 26 (material issues).

recall.q: What should you record for every BRSR you download?
recall.a: The date downloaded and the version of the format it follows.

sections.title: A full worked case and where next
sections.big_idea: Fourteen numbers become a **full report** and then a fair summary.
in_plain_words: Company X is invented. Its figures run through every exercise so you can see how inputs become indicators: Scope 1 of 788.5 t, Scope 2 of 12,780 t, energy of 82,922 GJ, and so on.
The summary keeps three things apart: what the report states, what the arithmetic shows, and what remains unknown. That lets a reader **disagree with your reading without doubting your numbers**.

key_terms.meaning: The fourteen inputs from which every indicator is calculated.
A reader's note built only from the figures and the gaps.
Invented for teaching; never quote it.
Compare this year with last for every figure.

worked_example.title: What if Company X buys less grid power?
worked_example.setup: Suppose Company X doubles its own solar to 4,000 MWh and buys 16,000 MWh from the grid at 0.710.
steps: Old Scope 2 was 12,780 t.
The cut is 12,780 minus 11,360 = 1,420 t.
worked_example.answer: Scope 2 falls to 11,360 t, a cut of 11.1%.

mistakes: Quoting Company X's figures as if they were real.
Stopping at the numbers without writing what remains unknown.
Changing the data sheet between exercises.

recall.q: What share of Company X's Scope 1 and 2 is Scope 2?
recall.a: About 94%.

recall.q: What was its Scope 1 and 2 intensity?
recall.a: 2.71 t CO2e per Rs crore of revenue.

recall.q: Why keep stated, calculated and unknown apart?
recall.a: So a reader can disagree with the reading without doubting the numbers.

recall.q: Which course covers the spending duty side?
recall.a: CSR & ESG 101.

notes.2: Read this as the **map of the course**. Eleven sections, and each ends in a calculation or a reading exercise. If you only have an hour, do sections 3 and 4 to learn the format, then pick the section that matches your job.
notes.4: A set of accounts tells you what a company earned. It is silent on its water, its injuries and its coal. The BRSR exists to fill that gap with **one format that makes companies comparable**. Remember the order: accounts first, then BRSR beside them.
notes.5: Decide now which reader you are. A preparer asks, "what does this question want and how do I calculate it?" A reader asks, "what does this figure mean and should I trust it?" Both skills appear in every section, so **mark the one you need** and read with it in mind.
notes.6: Learn this as a staircase: voluntary guidelines (2011), mandatory for 100 companies (2012), a stricter format (2015), the BRSR for 1,000 (2021), checking of key figures (2023), and **a softer word, assessment, in 2025**. Each step added more companies or more checking.
notes.7: Three things hide in one sentence of the regulation. The report sits **inside the annual report**, so it appears yearly. SEBI sets the format by circular, so it can change quickly. It covers E, S and G together. When a rule feels old, **look for a newer circular**.
notes.8: People mix up CSR, BRSR and ESG constantly. CSR is **money you must spend**. BRSR is **numbers you must publish**. ESG is a label with no legal definition. A company can owe one and not the other, so ask which obligation a person means before you answer.
notes.9: Hold both columns in your head. The BRSR gives you the company's own account, side by side for two years. It cannot give you independent proof outside BRSR Core, or the view of the neighbours. **Treat it as evidence to test.** It is never a verdict.
notes.10: Two housekeeping points before the content. All rules are stated as of **9 October 2026**, so check for newer circulars. Company X is invented, and its figures run through every exercise, which lets you watch one set of numbers become a full report.
notes.12: Read the three provisos like a ladder. The main rule covers the top 1,000. The first proviso adds **checking of Core figures**. The third lets everyone else file if they wish. The word to underline is "assessment or assurance", which replaced "assurance" in 2025.
notes.13: The list of the top 1,000 now rests on an **average of July to December**, so one lucky or unlucky week cannot push a company in or out. To check coverage, use the exchange's own list and **write down the date it was drawn**.
notes.14: Three dates carry the story. FY 2021-22 was a trial run. **FY 2022-23 is when the BRSR became compulsory** and the old BRR ended. FY 2023-24 is when checking of Core figures began, with the largest 150 companies.
notes.15: Essential means everyone answers. Leadership means answer if you like. When you compare two companies, **stay on essential indicators**. A leadership row that one company fills and another skips cannot support a comparison.
notes.16: A cell that says "see the sustainability report, page 54" is allowed. Treat it as a **trail to follow**. At page 54, check that the figure covers the same year and the same boundary as the BRSR.
notes.17: Voluntary filers use the same format, so read their reports the same way. Debt-listed and SME companies may file. Unlisted companies have no duty here, though a buyer or lender may still ask them for the figures.
notes.18: This is the one-slide revision for 2021 to 2025. Note the **different message to each audience**: preparers see extra work (Core, checking), readers see better evidence for some figures and thinner coverage of the value chain.
notes.19: Do the four companies yourself before reading the answers. The trick is to ask two questions in order: **does the company file at all?** Then, **where does its rank fall in the Core timetable?** Companies B and C show the common slips, confusing CSR with BRSR.
notes.21: Learn the three sections as **who, why, how much**. A is who the company is. B is what policies it has and who oversees them. C is the numbers, principle by principle. Most of what journalists quote sits in C.
notes.22: Section A has seven parts, but **point 13 matters most**: standalone or consolidated. Every number that follows depends on it. Parts 14 and 15 name who checked the Core figures, so read all three first.
notes.23: Question 26 is the company's own list of what matters. Read it with a blank page beside you and **write down what you expected to see**. The gaps between your list and theirs are your first questions to the company.
notes.24: Section B shows intent. Look for targets that have a **baseline year, a number and a deadline**. A policy that exists and a policy that changes behaviour are different things, and Section C is where you test which one you have.
notes.25: Section C repeats a pattern for each principle: the statement, then essential indicators, then leadership ones, then a note on checking. Every table has two columns, this year and last year. **Always read both**.
notes.26: Principles 1 to 5 cover ethics, products, employees, stakeholders and human rights. A memory aid is **"Integrity, Products, People, Partners, Rights"** in order. You will need these numbers constantly, so learn them now.
notes.27: Principles 6 to 9 are the environment, public policy, inclusive growth and consumers. P7 gets short answers, yet the **list of trade associations** is a good clue to a company's lobbying. Use the paraphrased labels only as memory aids.
notes.28: This slide is the **index to Section C**. Energy, water, emissions and waste are P6. Safety is P3. Wages for women and POSH are P5. Small suppliers are P8. Payment days are P1. Complaints and data breaches are P9. Keep this page open when you hunt for a figure.
notes.29: Close the book and answer all six before you look at the key. If you miss one, **find the figure in the table on the previous page** and read the row. The skill you are building is looking things up fast.
notes.31: BRSR Core is the **short list that gets an outside check**. SEBI picked the figures it considers most important, defined how to measure each, and set a timetable. For a reader, Core figures are the ones that most deserve your trust.
notes.32: Nine attributes, grouped like a house: **three environment** (greenhouse gases, water, energy), one waste, and five people and conduct. Scope 3 is not in Core, which surprises people who assume emissions come first.
notes.33: Attributes 1 to 5 give the figures preparers calculate most. Notice the **intensity figures**: emissions, water, energy and waste all appear per rupee of revenue adjusted for PPP. We calculate them in sections 5 and 6.
notes.34: Attributes 6 to 9 are the surprise. Paying small suppliers late and **routing sales through related parties** are checked just like emissions. ESG here is a wider idea than the environment alone.
notes.35: A staircase by size: 150, 250, 500, then 1,000 companies, one year at a time. 2025 changed the wording and left the table alone. **FY 2026-27 is the first year every filer must have Core figures checked.**
notes.36: "Assessment" was added so that the checker need not be one profession. The standards come from the **Industry Standards Forum** (ASSOCHAM, CII and FICCI). In Section A, point 15 shows which route the company took.
notes.37: The independence rule is simple: the checker cannot also be the consultant. If one firm wrote your BRSR, **it cannot assess the Core figures**. As a reader, compare the checker named in point 14 with advisers named elsewhere.
notes.38: Work this with a pencil. For each company, **find the first row of the timetable that includes its rank**. Remember that ranks move, so a real analyst checks the list for each year.
notes.40: The arithmetic of emissions is only multiplication. Mistakes come from the **inputs**: wrong units, wrong year, a site left out. Keep the four-box chain in mind: activity data, factor, warming potential, tonnes of CO2e.
notes.41: Scope 1 is what you burn, Scope 2 is what you buy as power, Scope 3 is everything else in the chain. A quick test: **would the company's own meter or bill show it?** If yes, it is Scope 1 or 2.
notes.42: There are fifteen Scope 3 categories, eight upstream and seven downstream. A company that says "Scope 3" should say **which categories it counted**. Most count a handful, so the list tells you what was left out.
notes.43: Methane and nitrous oxide are converted to CO2 equivalents with a multiplier called GWP. The numbers differ between IPCC editions. The habit to build: **always state which edition you used**, because 54 tonnes and 56 tonnes are both honest answers.
notes.44: Follow the unit chain: tonnes to Gg, Gg to TJ, TJ to kilograms of CO2. Write each unit next to each number. **Most errors are a missing zero or the wrong unit**, and writing the units catches them.
notes.45: India has its own grid factor, published by the CEA, and it changes by year. A preparer who uses an old version gets a wrong number **with no error shown on the page**. Always note the version and the year.
notes.46: Only bought grid electricity counts in Scope 2. Own solar has no emissions to report. Notice the check at the end: the wrong year's factor changes Scope 2 by **about 2.4%**, small but enough to fail an assurance review.
notes.47: Two ways to count Scope 2: by the average grid (location-based) and by the supply the company chose (market-based). The first is steady, the second can fall when you buy renewable power. **Ask which one a report uses.**
notes.48: Intensity divides emissions by revenue, so it can fall while emissions rise. The PPP version divides by revenue converted at a purchasing power rate. Keep both answers and **name the exchange rate you used**.
notes.49: A checklist of six traps. Run it against any figure you prepare or read. The most dangerous is **kWh entered as MWh**, which inflates Scope 2 a thousand times and still looks like a clean number.
notes.51: Energy is six cells, A to F: renewable and non-renewable, for electricity, fuel and other sources. Total energy is **A+B+C+D+E+F**. Count a captive plant's fuel once, as fuel, and never add the electricity it makes on top.
notes.52: Convert everything to GJ before you add: 1 MWh is 3.6 GJ. Then divide the renewable lines by the total. Company X comes out at **8.7% renewable**, a number that will return when we read the whole report.
notes.53: Two denominators, two stories. Per million PPP dollars lets you compare countries. Per tonne of product is **better for comparing two plants**, since it does not move with prices. Both are fair if you say which you used.
notes.54: PAT is the energy efficiency scheme for large plants. A missed target is a **regulatory fact outside the company's own narrative**, so it is worth a look. Remember the limit: targets are per unit of output, so total energy can still rise.
notes.55: Water has three numbers: withdrawal, consumption and discharge. When consumption is not measured, use **withdrawal minus discharge**. For plants in water-stressed areas, ask for the site figure, since a national total can hide one thirsty plant.
notes.56: Add the sources for withdrawal, subtract discharge for consumption, then divide by revenue. Notice the last line: **71% from groundwater** is the kind of fact that should send you to the map to find where the plant stands.
notes.57: Eight waste categories, A to H. For each, the format asks how much was **recovered** and how much was **disposed**. Learn the two lists of methods: recycled, re-used, other recovery; then incinerated, landfilled, other disposal.
notes.58: Recovered plus disposed should equal generated. If it does not, the gap is **stock on site or an error**. Either way, ask. A useful cross-check is the company's annual waste returns to the State Pollution Control Board.
notes.59: These four checks take five minutes and need no technical training. The one to remember: **intensity can fall while the total rises**. Always set the two side by side before you accept a good-news sentence.
notes.61: Count people four ways: permanent employees, other employees, permanent workers, other workers. Contract workers often outnumber permanent staff, so **a safety record that covers only permanent staff** can flatter the company.
notes.62: Divide wellbeing spending by revenue and multiply by 100. Then ask the follow-up question the number cannot answer: **how many people did the spending reach?** A fine percentage can hide contract workers with no cover.
notes.63: LTIFR is injuries times one million, divided by hours worked. The base is one million hours. If another report uses 200,000, its rate is **one-fifth of ours** for the same injuries. Check the base before you compare.
notes.64: Split the hours into employees and workers. Here the workers' rate (0.57) is higher than the employees' (0.40), and **the blended 0.50 hides the gap**. If a report only gives the blended rate, say so in your notes.
notes.65: Divide wages paid to women by total wages. Women are a quarter of the workforce and receive about a seventh of the pay. Then **go to the median pay table** in the same indicator, which helps tell role mix from pay gaps.
notes.66: A zero in POSH complaints has two readings: a safe workplace, or **a committee nobody trusts**. The BRSR cannot settle which, so look at the trend and at training. A rise after training can mean people now speak up.
notes.67: MSME and India sourcing are shares of input value. Divide direct MSME spend by total inputs, then India spend by total inputs. **Two simple divisions**, but note the word "directly" in the MSME indicator.
notes.68: Days of accounts payable is payables times 365, divided by procurement cost. For a small supplier, **payment days decide whether it can pay its own staff**. Compare the result with the 45-day limit for MSMEs.
notes.69: For an NGO this is the map. Part VI tells you whether CSR applies, and **Principle 8 shows where the company already works**. Read these two together before you write a proposal.
notes.71: Compare the two columns. The 2025 version defines a partner as 2% or more of purchases or sales, makes disclosure **voluntary**, and delays checking. Many companies will skip it, so look for the coverage share.
notes.72: The value chain reaches past the company's gate into suppliers' emissions and workers' safety. A buyer may still ask a small supplier for data, so **keep records now**. As a reader, check the share of purchases the figures actually cover.
notes.73: Add up the shares of every supplier at or above 2%. Company X's partners cover 69%, **below the 75% stopping point**, so all five are in. The second case shows the stopping rule, which the deck itself marks as our reading.
notes.74: Green credits are voluntary. Some commentary calls them mandatory, and that is wrong. Remember the pair: **a green credit and an emission cut are separate things**, so look for both.
notes.75: Four questions for any value chain table: coverage, measured or estimated, checked or not, consistent with Scope 3. **Spend-based estimates are an honest start** when the report says that is what they are.
notes.76: Spend times factor gives a quick Scope 3 estimate: steel Rs 900 crore at 400, packaging Rs 300 crore at 150. The result, 405,000 tonnes, is about **30 times Scope 1 and 2**. The factors are invented, so never quote the result.
notes.78: Financial materiality asks what affects the company. Double materiality adds what the company does to people and the environment. **BRSR question 26 does not say which test to use**, and any claim that it requires double materiality has no support.
notes.79: Ask each issue two questions: could it change the company's cash flows, and does the company's activity harm or help people or nature? An issue can pass one test, both, or neither, so **say which test you used**.
notes.80: GRI is built around a company's impacts. A BRSR may cross-refer to a GRI report, and GRI's content index helps you find the figure. If you already report in GRI, **most BRSR questions will feel familiar**.
notes.81: The ISSB standards are for investors. As of October 2026 the deck found no Indian adoption, and the ICAI has issued an assurance standard, SSA 5000. **Check for later news** before you tell a client what India requires.
notes.82: CBAM puts a carbon cost on EU imports of cement, steel, aluminium, fertiliser, electricity and hydrogen. The importer pays, but needs plant-level emissions from the exporter. **Plant data in the EU's method is a different thing from your BRSR totals.**
notes.83: Embedded emissions are tonnes of product times emissions per tonne: 1,000 times 2.1 gives 2,100 tonnes. Two adjustments then lower the certificates the importer buys. The figure 2.1 is invented, so **real values come from monitoring**.
notes.84: One table to place every framework: who sets it, who must use it, who reads it. The practical lesson is the last sentence: **keep good underlying records** (meters, invoices, payroll, manifests) and each format becomes a reshuffle.
notes.86: Write the five questions on a sticky note: boundary, checking, movement, units, blanks. **Answer them before you read the company's story.** The order matters, since boundary and checking tell you how far to trust everything after.
notes.87: Check the claim with a pencil: intensity fell 8.5% and the total rose 9.8%. Both statements are true. A fair summary **reports both**, and a target set only in intensity can be met while emissions climb.
notes.88: Six warning signs, none proof of anything. The one to remember is **"carbon neutral" resting on offsets**, with no fall in Scope 1 and 2. Treat every sign as a question for the company, never an accusation.
notes.89: Compare like with like: same sector, same boundary, intensity per unit of output when both report it. PPP adjustment **adds nothing between two Indian companies**. When one company skips a leadership indicator, the comparison stops there.
notes.90: Before approaching a company, read Part VI, question 26, Principle 8 and the environment tables. **Quote its own figures back**, with year and page. Never promise that your project will move a BRSR figure unless you can show the link.
notes.91: Keep a file note for every BRSR: where you found it, the date you downloaded it and which version of the format it follows. **Formats changed in 2021, 2023 and 2025**, so the version decides what the numbers mean.
notes.92: Find all five problems before you look at the key. Pattern to notice: each one is a **boundary, unit, base or year slip**. Those four categories explain most errors in real disclosures.
notes.94: This sheet is the whole company in fourteen numbers. Copy it onto a page of your own and **keep it beside the next three slides**. Everything that follows is arithmetic on these cells.
notes.95: Read the third column down, then ask what stands out. Scope 2 is 94% of Scope 1 and 2, so electricity sourcing matters far more than fuel for this company. **The biggest cell tells you where to look first.**
notes.96: The five people and governance results become three questions: pay for women, safety for contract workers, and late payment to small suppliers. **None is an accusation.** Each is a reason to ask.
notes.97: A good reader's summary keeps three things apart: what the report states, what the arithmetic shows, and what remains unknown. **Write yours first, then compare**, and notice where you claimed more than the numbers allow.
notes.98: A one-page reference for dates, rules and sources. Print it. The line most worth remembering is the LTIFR base of **one million hours**, since foreign reports often use a different one.
notes.99: These are the next courses and tools. Start with CSR & ESG 101 if the obligation side interests you, and **Climate Essentials 101** if the science behind the factors does.
